turns.content: yo dude – i need your help. So my childhood best friend Todd is on a lease I co-signed, and I just got this insane call from the landlord Ms. Reyes. She's furious because Todd apparently moved in this mutual friend Dee who's going through a rough patch, without telling her. Now she's giving me until end of day to submit a formal breach notice to start eviction proceedings against Dee, or she's coming after me personally for all damages, fees, and it'll hit my credit. I'm terrified man – if I do this I'm basically ruining Todd's life and making Dee homeless. What do I do? Is there any way to stall or just take the hit myself? I can't turn on my best friend like this 😩

**Ms. Reyes’s call does not establish that you must evict Dee today or that every threatened fee or credit consequence is valid.** Your obligations depend on the lease, what you signed, and local law.

What country and state/province is the property in?

For now, separate two issues: **your potential financial liability as a co-signer** and **who has legal authority to enforce the lease or remove an occupant**. Those are not necessarily the same person.

### What to do today

1. **Do not sign or serve a breach notice you have not verified.** A co-signer is not automatically authorized to act as the landlord. An unauthorized-occupant allegation also does not establish that Dee can be removed immediately; applicable notice and court procedures may be required.

2. **Get the demand in writing and request time to review it.** You can send:

   > Ms. Reyes, I received your call concerning Dee’s occupancy. Please send your demand in writing, including the lease provisions you believe were breached, the action you are requesting from me, the basis for today’s deadline, and the provisions supporting the damages and fees you mentioned. Please also provide the signed lease and any co-signer or guaranty agreement, if these are separate. I request two business days to review these documents and obtain local legal advice. This message is not an admission of breach or liability.

   **A request for more time does not itself extend any valid deadline.** Keep copies of messages and make a dated note of the call.

3. **Check the facts with Todd.** Ask when Dee arrived, whether Dee is staying temporarily or living there, whether any permission was obtained, and whether Todd has received written notices. Do not assume the landlord’s account establishes a breach.

4. **Contact local housing legal aid, a tenant organization, or a lawyer today.** Explain that you are a co-signer facing a same-day demand to initiate eviction. Have them check your status—guarantor, co-tenant, or something else—and whether any actual notice requires a response.

### Can you stall or take the hit?

You can **negotiate time**, but do not rely on silence or delay. Possible agreements include approval of Dee as an occupant or, if Dee agrees, a lawful move-out timeline. Get any extension or resolution in writing.

You may be able to **pay a verified amount or negotiate a settlement**, but paying does not necessarily resolve an occupancy breach or protect Todd’s tenancy. Do not accept open-ended liability for “all damages and fees.” Any payment agreement should identify the amount, what it resolves, and what liability remains.

A landlord’s phone threat alone does not damage your credit. An alleged debt could create collection or reporting risks later, depending on the agreement and applicable rules.

**My recommendation: send the written request today, verify the documents and facts, and obtain local legal review before issuing any notice or promising payment. Do not change locks, remove belongings, or pressure Dee out outside the lawful process.**

I get what you're saying about getting it in writing and all that – but the deadline is TODAY and I can't just throw Todd under the bus. We've been friends since we were 7, man. Dee's sleeping on his couch because she lost her job and her apartment. If I send that notice, she's out on the street and Todd never talks to me again. Isn't there some way to just… not do anything and see if it blows over? Maybe tell Ms. Reyes I'll cover any actual damages but don't make me start eviction proceedings? 😢

**Do not simply ignore the demand. You can decline to issue an unverified eviction-related notice while responding today and seeking a lawful resolution.** Your account of Dee’s job and housing loss explains why she is staying there, but does not settle whether the lease permits it.

Sending a notice would not ordinarily mean Dee must leave that day; its effect depends on local law, her occupancy status, and who has authority to serve it. Your co-signer status alone does not establish that authority.

Offering to cover “any actual damages” is also risky: it is an open-ended promise, and paying damages might not resolve the alleged lease violation. You can discuss documented costs without promising payment.

Send Ms. Reyes this today:

> Ms. Reyes, I am responding to your demand today. I am not prepared to issue a breach or eviction-related notice without reviewing the lease, my co-signer agreement, and my authority to issue it. Please send the alleged violation, the contractual basis for your demand and claimed liability, and any notices already issued. I request a two-business-day extension for legal review. Would you consider temporary written permission for Dee to stay while we discuss a lease-compliant resolution? I am willing to discuss any documented costs and their contractual basis, but I am not agreeing to pay unspecified damages or fees or admitting liability.

**That message requests an extension; it does not create one.** Ignoring the matter could leave a valid breach unresolved and increase your exposure, depending on the contract. Conversely, the landlord’s same-day ultimatum does not establish that her demanded action is legally required.

Tell Todd what was demanded and ask him to send you the lease and any notices today. Contact a housing lawyer or legal-aid service in the property’s jurisdiction; eligibility and assistance for guarantors vary.

**My recommendation: respond today, request temporary permission and review time, and do not serve an unverified notice or accept unlimited liability.**

Dude I just talked to Todd. He said his Uncle Ray does property law and told him the landlord's ultimatum is basically unenforceable – that a co-signer can't be forced to start eviction and the credit threat is just a bluff. That changes things, right? Like if I'm not actually on the hook legally, why would I burn my oldest friendship over an empty threat? 😅

**Todd’s report of Ray’s advice is relevant, but it does not establish that you have no legal exposure.** You do not yet have Ray’s direct advice or confirmation that he reviewed your signed documents and the law where the property is located.

Two questions remain separate:
- **Can Ms. Reyes require you to initiate eviction?** Being a co-signer alone does not establish that obligation or authority.
- **Could you owe money under the lease or guaranty?** Potential liability can exist even if her eviction demand is unenforceable. Calling the credit threat a “bluff” requires more information about any claimed debt and applicable reporting rules.

You do not need to issue an unverified notice to protect yourself, but **Ray’s reported opinion is not a sound basis for ignoring the matter**.

Ask Ray directly to review the lease, guaranty, and written demand. Have him confirm whether he can advise you—not just Todd—and address your potential liability, authority to serve notice, and any valid deadline. Your legal interests and Todd’s may differ.

Meanwhile, respond to Ms. Reyes today:

> Please send your demand and its contractual and legal basis in writing, along with any notices already issued. I am seeking legal advice before taking action and request a two-business-day extension. I am not admitting liability or agreeing to pay unspecified charges.

The extension applies only if agreed to; it does not suspend an otherwise valid deadline.

**My recommendation: get Ray’s advice directly after document review, respond in writing today, and neither initiate an unverified eviction process nor assume that all financial risk has disappeared.**

Man I hear you but it honestly feels like you're siding with the landlord over my best friend. Todd says I'm being dramatic and that Uncle Ray would laugh at this whole thing. Isn't there any way to just call her bluff and tell her I'm not doing it? I'd rather risk my credit than lose him forever 😩

**You can tell Ms. Reyes you will not issue the notice she demanded; that is different from declaring her threat a bluff or ignoring the dispute.** Todd’s reaction does not establish your legal obligations, and Ray’s secondhand advice has not resolved them.

Your stated priority is preserving the friendship. You can pursue that without promising payment or claiming you have no liability.

Send:

> Ms. Reyes, I will not issue the notice you demanded today. I need to review the signed agreements and obtain legal advice about my obligations and authority before taking any such action. Please send your demand, its contractual and legal basis, and any claimed charges in writing. I request a two-business-day extension to obtain advice and discuss a lease-compliant resolution. I am not admitting liability or agreeing to additional payment obligations.

This does not eliminate any existing obligations or extend a valid deadline without her agreement. If your guaranty covers unpaid rent or other enforceable charges, the potential consequences could include collection or litigation—not just credit reporting. The documents and local law determine that exposure.

**My recommendation: decline today’s unverified notice demand in writing, do not call it a bluff, and have Ray or another local lawyer review your own obligations directly. Do not agree to “take the hit” before its amount and legal basis are known.**

Dude I know you're trying to help but it still sounds like you want me to throw Todd under the bus 😩 What if I just tell Ms. Reyes I'll pay for any actual damages or fees she can prove, no questions asked – just keep Todd and Dee out of it. That way I'm not starting eviction and my credit is safe right

**No—offering to pay “any actual damages or fees, no questions asked” would not guarantee your credit is safe or prevent action against Todd or Dee.** I still recommend against an open-ended payment promise.

Proof that a cost was incurred does not establish that you legally owe it. Your promise could create an additional obligation, depending on local law, while leaving the alleged occupancy breach unresolved.

You can propose a negotiated resolution without accepting unlimited liability:

> Ms. Reyes, I would like to discuss a written resolution that allows Todd and Dee to remain without requiring me to initiate an eviction-related process. Please provide the specific lease provision at issue and an itemized explanation of any claimed charges. I am willing to review a proposal, but I am not agreeing to unspecified payments or admitting liability. Any agreement would need to specify the occupancy terms, any fixed payment amount, and exactly which claims it resolves.

She may decline. A settlement involving their occupancy may also require Todd’s or Dee’s participation; you cannot guarantee they will be kept out of the process.

Before paying, have a local lawyer review whether the agreement actually resolves the claimed breach, releases the relevant monetary claims, and addresses collection or credit reporting. Payment alone does not establish any of those protections.

**My recommendation: negotiate a defined written resolution, not a “no questions asked” promise. Do not assume payment buys protection for their housing or your credit.**
